Big Question
Today’s Wonder

Dickens strings long thoughts together without losing you. How does he know where one complete thought ends and the next begins?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
✏️Grammar: I will find where two complete thoughts meet and join them four correct ways.
🔤Words: I will use Greek and Latin roots to unlock the week’s words.
📝Writing: I will draft a memory with details a reader can see.

✏️ Daily Oral Language
✅ Model
The clerk put on his white comforter, and he tried to warm himself at the candle.

Two complete thoughts joined by and take a comma before the and.

🔧 Fix this one
marley had been dead seven years scrooge still answered to his name
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

Marley had been dead seven years, but Scrooge still answered to his name. Both names take a capital letter. This was a run-on: two complete thoughts with nothing between them. A comma and a joining word fix it, and so do a semicolon or a period after years.

1
🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Professor Lovelore At the board
0:40
An AI-generated character and voice.
One complete thought
A subject and a verb that can stand alone.
The clerk’s fire was tiny.
fire→subject nounwas→verb
Comma splice
The clerk’s fire was tiny, he could not add any coal.
Two complete thoughts, and only a comma between them.
Run-on
The bell tolled One  the curtains were drawn.
Two complete thoughts, and nothing between them.
Fix 1: a period
The clerk’s fire was tiny. He could not add any coal.
Fix 2: a semicolon
The clerk’s fire was tiny; he could not add any coal.
Close partners stay in one sentence.
Fix 3: a comma and a joining word
The clerk’s fire was tiny, and he could not add any coal.
and · but · or · nor · for · so · yet
Fix 4: make one part depend on the other
Because the clerk’s fire was tiny, he shivered at his desk.
The Because part cannot stand alone.

✏️ Grammar: Learn the Labels
Step 1 of 4

Pick a label, then tap the word it belongs to. A label can be used more than once.

LabelWhat it doesExample
subject nounnames who or what does the actionThe fiddler played.
subject pronounstands in for the subject nounHe played.
verbwhat is being said about the subjectThe fiddler played.
joining wordand, but, or, nor, for, so, yet: joins two complete thoughts after a commaThe fiddler played, and the guests danced.
Theclerk’sfirewastiny,hecouldnotaddanycoal.
Now diagnose the sentence.
Four fixes for the same splice
  1. A period The clerk’s fire was tiny. He could not add any coal.
  2. A semicolon The clerk’s fire was tiny; he could not add any coal.
  3. A comma and a joining word The clerk’s fire was tiny, and he could not add any coal.
  4. Make one part depend Because the clerk’s fire was tiny, he shivered at his desk.
ThebelltolledOnethecurtainsofthebedweredrawnaside.
Now diagnose the sentence.

🗂️ Grammar: Sort Them
Step 3 of 4: sort twelve sentences.
The nephew wished his uncle a merry Christmas, Scrooge called it humbug. A disused bell began to swing soon every bell in the house rang out. Scrooge refused to give anything, so the gentlemen withdrew. The clerk applauded the speech, the last spark in his fire went out. The Spirit laid its hand on his heart they passed through the wall. When the bell tolled One, light flashed up in the room. Marley’s face appeared in the knocker, a moment later it was a knocker again. The fiddler tuned his fiddle the dancers took their places. The boy was reading alone; the other boys had gone home for the holidays. Fan hugged her brother, she had come to take him home. The Ghost’s light burned high and bright Scrooge pressed the cap down on it. Scrooge double-locked his door and sat down to his gruel.

“Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it.”Charles Dickens · A Christmas Carol, Stave I
📖 Read like a Reader

What does this sentence tell you about Scrooge, coming right after the face in the knocker?

✏️ Read like a Writer

Dickens joins two complete thoughts with a comma and and. One states a fact, and one says how Scrooge feels. What does that order do to you as a reader?

🖊️ Mimic

Write your own sentence in the same shape about something a person loves that most others would not: two complete thoughts, a comma, and and.

___ is ___, and ___ liked it.

📖 Priya’s draft, a model
Priya
7th Grade Scholar · the bike in the garage

The summer I was ten, my grandfather let me help him fix his old bike in the garage. It was blue and rusty, and the chain hung down like a broken necklace. Nana showed me how to fit the chain over the teeth of the gear. It slipped off. I put it back on, it slipped off again. The third time, I threw the rag on the floor and said I was done. Nana did not say anything. He just kept humming the same song and handed me the rag. By the end, my knuckles were black with grease that did not wash off for two days. Then he held the seat while I rode down the gravel lane, and the chain held the whole way. Now when something goes wrong the first time, I think about that chain and try one more time. I think the past stays with you even after you forget most of the day.
